literal_meaning: Bread is not rice / not a meal

seo.meta_title: Why Bread Isn't a Meal in Korea | 밥 vs 빵 Explained
seo.meta_description: You say you had a sandwich for lunch and a Korean replies 'So you haven't eaten?' Why 밥 means a real meal, and what to say instead.

ai_failure.situation: Your Korean partner's mom asks 밥 먹었니? You had a sandwich, so you say 네, 빵 먹었어요. She frowns: 빵이 무슨 밥이야, and starts cooking.
ai_failure.ai_mistake: Translates 밥 as 'meal' and treats any food as an answer, so her reaction seems confusing or even rude.
ai_failure.why_it_fails: 밥 means both 'cooked rice' and 'a meal'. For many Koreans, especially older ones, a real meal means rice with soup and side dishes. Bread, ramen or snacks are something you 'got by on', not a meal — so she heard 'I haven't eaten properly'.

natural_solution.rule: 밥 = a proper meal, usually rice. If you had bread or noodles, say you 'got by' (때웠어요) — and expect to be fed.

alternatives.context: 'I just got by on some bread' — honest, and Koreans will understand you haven't had a real meal
'I haven't had a proper meal yet'
Use only if you really had a full meal — otherwise elders may feel misled

nuance: There's a saying that Koreans run on 밥심, 'rice power'. Rice is so central that 밥 became the word for any meal, and asking 밥 먹었어? is a way of caring for someone. Not every Korean thinks bread doesn't count — younger people eat sandwiches for lunch all the time — but with parents, in-laws and older coworkers, assume bread, ramen and coffee are 간식 (snacks). It's also why a Korean host may keep offering food after you've 'eaten'.
